```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%", dpi = 96)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(bdhs)
```

DHS indicators look simple ("percentage of births delivered in a health
facility") but each one hides decisions. Which births count, from which
time window, with which weight, and how should ever-married samples or
missing codes be handled? bdhs encodes these decisions once, following the
DHS Program's definitions. Each indicator was then checked against the
official estimates using real BDHS files.

The examples below use synthetic data from `bdhs_simulate()`, so the numbers
are random. With your own data from `bdhs_read()` they reproduce the BDHS
reports.

## The indicator library

```{r}
ind <- bdhs_indicator_list()
nrow(ind)
table(ind$topic)
ind[ind$topic == "maternal_health", c("id", "label", "recode", "api_id")]
```

Every indicator has an `id`, the recode it is computed from, and the DHS
Program API id of the matching official estimate (`api_id`), which is also
in the bundled `bdhs_indicators`. The `definition` and `notes` columns say
exactly what is computed:

```{r}
x <- ind[ind$id == "rh_del_skilled", ]
writeLines(strwrap(c(x$definition, "", x$notes), width = 76))
```

## Estimating

`bdhs_estimate()` takes a recode data frame and indicator ids. It builds the
survey design (`bdhs_design()`) and returns estimates with standard errors,
confidence intervals and denominators:

```{r}
kr <- bdhs_simulate(2022, "KR")
bdhs_estimate(kr, c("rh_anc_4plus", "rh_del_facility", "rh_del_csection"))
```

Add `by` for subgroups. Labelled variables are shown with their labels:

```{r}
est <- bdhs_estimate(kr, c("rh_del_facility", "rh_del_csection"), by = "v190")
est
```

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2}
plot(est)
```

A few details are handled for you:

* **Percentages** are on the 0-100 scale, as in DHS reports (`scale`).
  Confidence intervals are computed on the logit scale, so they stay
  between 0 and 100 (`ci_method = "wald"` gives symmetric intervals).
* **All-women indicators.** BDHS interviews only ever-married women, so
  indicators about all women, such as child marriage or teenage
  childbearing, use the DHS all-woman factors through a ratio estimator. The
  factor that matches a single `by` variable is used (`awfactu` for
  residence, `awfactr` for division, and so on).
* **Medians** (age at first marriage) use the DHS interpolation and
  jackknife standard errors.
* **Round differences.** Some definitions change between rounds, for
  example who counts as a skilled provider, the 2022 short questionnaire, or
  solar electricity in 2022. These are built into each indicator. An
  indicator that a round did not collect is skipped with a warning.

```{r}
ir <- bdhs_simulate(2022, "IR")
bdhs_estimate(ir, c("fp_cpr_modern", "fp_unmet_total", "ms_married_by_18", "ms_median_afm_20_49"))
```

### Pooled rounds

Pooled data (see `vignette("survey-design")`) are estimated round by round:

```{r}
pooled <- bdhs_pool(bdhs_simulate(2014, "KR", seed = 1), bdhs_simulate(2022, "KR", seed = 2))
bdhs_estimate(pooled, "rh_del_csection")
```

## Indicators as variables for modelling

`bdhs_add_indicators()` adds indicator columns to your data. They are 0/1
inside the denominator and `NA` outside it, so they are ready for
regression:

```{r}
kr2 <- bdhs_add_indicators(kr, "rh_del_csection")
des <- bdhs_design(kr2)
fit <- survey::svyglm(rh_del_csection ~ factor(v025) + factor(v106), design = des, family = quasibinomial())
round(coef(summary(fit)), 3)
```

## Fertility and mortality rates

Rates need the DHS synthetic-cohort methods. These are implemented natively,
with jackknife standard errors, and checked against the DHS.rates package
and the official values.

```{r}
bdhs_fertility(ir)                         # TFR, last 3 years
bdhs_fertility(ir, type = "asfr")[, c("age_group", "estimate", "se")]
```

The births recode (or the birth history in the women's recode) gives
childhood mortality for the five years before the survey:

```{r}
br <- bdhs_simulate(2022, "BR")
bdhs_mortality(br)[, c("indicator", "estimate", "se", "ci_low", "ci_high")]
```

Both functions accept `by` for subgroups and a `period` argument (in months
for fertility, in years for mortality).

## Validation: does it reproduce the BDHS reports?

`bdhs_validate()` computes every indicator it can from your data and compares
it with the official value bundled in `bdhs_indicators`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
kr <- bdhs_read(2017, "KR")
bdhs_validate(kr)
```

Use it as a first check on your copy of the data. Simulated data are random,
so they are not expected to pass.

The package itself was validated this way using real files from every round
the maintainer had (KR for all rounds except 1996-97, and IR, PR and BR for
2017-18 and 2022). `bdhs_validation_record()` holds the results, which are
national aggregates only:

```{r}
rec <- bdhs_validation_record()
summary_tab <- aggregate(pass ~ survey_id, rec, function(x) sprintf("%d / %d", sum(x), length(x)))
names(summary_tab)[2] <- "passed"
summary_tab
```

The three comparisons that fail are known and documented:

```{r}
rec[!rec$pass, ]
```

* Women's anthropometry in 2022 must come from the household member file
  (PR). It covers all women in the biomarker subsample, while the women's
  file covers ever-married women only. Use `bdhs_estimate(pr, "nt_wm_thin")`.
* Exclusive breastfeeding in 2007 is 42.9% against the official 49.8%. The
  cause is still under investigation.

### Things the validation taught us

* **2022 short questionnaire.** About a third of the 2022 women (10,091 of
  30,078) answered a short questionnaire (`sqtype == 2`) without
  family planning, marriage and empowerment questions. Counting them as "no"
  understates unmet need (6.7% instead of 10.0%) and child marriage (33.9%
  instead of 50.7%). bdhs restricts these indicators to the long
  questionnaire, as the DHS Program does.
* **No vaccination data in the 2022 children's file.** The vaccination
  variables of the 2022 KR are empty, and there are no official 2022
  vaccination estimates, so these indicators are unavailable for 2022.
* **Solar electricity.** The 2022 electricity indicator includes solar
  home systems (`sh132g`), as in the final report (99.4%).

The `validated` column of `bdhs_indicator_list()` lists, for each
indicator, the rounds in which it reproduced the official value. Indicators
without an official value have an empty list there: solid cooking fuel and
the 2011/2017-18 biomarker indicators (hypertension and diabetes). Use them
with care.

## Comparing with the official numbers

The official values are always one call away:

```{r}
bdhs_official("RH_DELA_C_CSC")[, c("year_label", "value", "ci_low", "ci_high")]
```

Your microdata estimates and the official values share the same
`indicator`/`api_id` link, so it is easy to put them side by side, or to map
your own estimates with `bdhs_map()`.
